rv.q: Rajiv Joseph's smart, savagely funny and visionary new work of American theater, whose presence on Broadway invites fanciful comparison to the titular beast.
Williams sinks his teeth into his meaty part, sometimes bending the script to serve his voice, not the other way around.

Joseph has written an evocative reflection on the alienation and absurdity of war, its psychological impact on both invader and invaded, the infinite reverberations of violent acts, and the deadly toll of war on faith and spirituality, culture and history.
This odd, enchanting play — which was a Pulitzer finalist last year — owes much of its magic to his lordly presence.
He's put himself at the drama's service, and if that means ceding the stage to Moayed, whose poignancy has only deepened, so be it.
The play is a meditation on war, guilt and the afterlife that mixes comedy and tragedy in ways that don't always work but are never less than interesting.
Robin Williams brings his manic energy to Rajiv Joseph's ambitious play about war, humanity and redemption, though the production struggles to find its theatrical footing.
Like the show in general, it doesn't deliver on its promise.
This weekend is your last chance to attend one of the weirdest, most remarkable performance pieces I’ve ever seen.
Williams almost fades into the foliage.
Nevertheless, Rajiv's intelligent drama, as staged by Moisés Kaufman, convincingly captures the chaos of Iraq immediately following the 2003 invasion.
Most of all, the sheer theatricality of Joseph's work makes it worth celebrating.
It is a troubled piece of star casting that, regretfully, ensures that the Broadway experience is dominated by issues tangential to Joseph's main points of worthy exploration.
For all of its offbeat perspective, "Bengal Tiger" has a message of agony and frustration that's all too familiar.
But the play doesn't hold up, eventually collapsing in a muddle of mental masturbation.
Bengal Tiger demands to be seen by people who care about humanity and art and their troubling devolutions in the 21st century.
Truly a haunted and haunting new drama, 'Bengal Tiger at the Baghdad Zoo' is an imaginative, even poetic, consideration of the American invasion of Iraq.
In an oblique way, it’s a straightforward and important commentary on the war in Iraq and an aesthetically elegant and moving play.

Rajiv Joseph’s script for "Bengal Tiger at the Baghdad Zoo" has a special request about the actor playing the title character. "The Tiger can be any age, although ideally, he is older, scrappy, past his prime, yet still tough," Joseph says. "His language is loose, casual, his profanity is second nature."

cn.t: Joseph's ambitious Iraq War drama earns praise for its intelligence and dark humor, but critics are mixed on its execution. Williams impresses in an unconventional role, though some question whether the existential meditation fully coheres.
